title: The Science of Not Knowing
sub: Grades 5–8 · Science · Ambiguity, dread and the brain’s alarm
objective: Students will learn that the brain’s first fear is the unknown. Poster 1 calls it **ambiguity aversion**: we would rather face a known danger than an unknown possibility, and uncertainty itself sets off the **amygdala**, the brain’s alarm system. Students will vote on the lab’s six *Known or Unknown?* choices, compare their class with the studies the exhibition reports, read those studies as scientists, and design a fair, kind experiment of their own.

objectives.heading: By the end of this lesson you will be able to:
objectives.why: Every day you are asked to trust a claim that begins “studies show.” Knowing what a study changed, measured and counted lets you judge it for yourself.

materials: A cardboard box with a hand-sized hole, and something harmless inside (a pinecone, as in the lab)
The *Show your class* page (page 3), projected or printed; *What Scares You?* online if you have a screen
A clock with a second hand; differentiated handouts, one per student
questions: Would you rather know exactly what is in the box, or not know? Why might not knowing feel worse?
Have you ever found that waiting for something was worse than the thing itself?
Why might the brain’s alarm ring for something it cannot see?
The haunted house visitors enjoyed a medium scare most. Why not the biggest?
questionsLabel: Questions to ask in front of the poster
connection: **Visit the exhibition:** poster 1, *Fear of the Unknown*, and the two tactile Mystery Fear Boxes in the case, whose contents change each week. **Online:** *What Scares You?* has the six choices, and a pulse you can tap.

steps.title: A box you can’t see into
script: Hold up the box. Read the poster: *“Put your hand in a box you can’t see into. Your heart races before you even touch anything. Why?”* Before a volunteer reaches in, everyone finds their pulse on the wrist or neck, as the lab’s *Take your own pulse* asks. The volunteer says what it feels like, then pulls out the pinecone. Ask: *“What did you imagine was in there? Was the waiting worse than the pinecone?”*

screen.question: Put your hand in a box you can’t see into. Your heart races before you even touch anything. Why?

steps.purpose: Feel the effect before naming it: the heart races before the hand touches anything.
students: Find your pulse on your wrist or neck.
What do you think is in the box?
Did your heart speed up while you waited?

steps.title: Take the vote
script: Read each of the six choices from the lab’s *Known or Unknown?* (page 3), but not the last column. Students vote with a hand for *known* or *unknown*; a student records the tally on the board.

screen.question: Would you rather know exactly what is in the box, or not know? Why might not knowing feel worse?

steps.purpose: Collect the class’s own data before showing what the studies found.
students: A shock for sure, or maybe a shock?
A strong shock now, or a weak one later?
Which box would you reach into?
Which jar would you bet on?
Fifteen minutes alone with your thoughts, or a button?
Which haunted house would you go into?

steps.title: What the studies found
script: Now reveal what the exhibition reports, one row at a time. Read the poster: *“Scientists call it “ambiguity aversion”—we’d rather face a known danger than an unknown possibility. In experiments, a 50% chance of a small electric shock stressed people out more than knowing for certain they’d get one.”* Where did the class match the studies?

screen.caption: Known or Unknown? The six choices in the lab, and what the exhibition reports

cells: A shock for sure, or maybe a shock?
A small electric shock, for certain.
A 50% chance of a small electric shock.
The 50% chance stressed people out more than the certain shock (poster 1).
A strong shock now, or a weak one later?
A stronger shock, right away.
A weaker shock, but you have to wait for it.
Some people chose the stronger shock right away rather than wait (poster 1).
Which box would you reach into?
A glass box with a spider you can see.
A box you can’t see into.
Not seeing sets off the brain’s alarm louder than seeing an actual spider (poster 1).
Which jar would you bet on?
50 red and 50 black marbles. Pull out a red one to win.
100 red and black marbles, in a mix nobody will tell you.
Most people pick the known mix, though nobody has said the mystery jar is worse: the Ellsberg paradox, 1961.
Fifteen minutes alone with your thoughts, or a button?
Sit alone in a bare room for 15 minutes, with nothing to do but think.
Sit there with a button that gives you a small electric shock, if you want one.
In a 2014 study, 12 of 18 men and 6 of 24 women shocked themselves at least once rather than just sit and think.
Which haunted house would you go into?
A haunted house that is only a little bit scary.
The scariest haunted house in the world.
In 2020, 110 visitors to a haunted house in Vejle, Denmark, wore heart-rate monitors. They enjoyed it most when scared a medium amount.

steps.purpose: Compare the class’s choices with the exhibition’s findings, choice by choice.
students: Did our class match the studies?
Which result surprises you most?

steps.title: The brain’s alarm
script: Read: *“Uncertainty itself sets off the amygdala (your brain’s alarm system). When you can’t see what’s in that box, your brain screams “THREAT!” louder than if you saw an actual spider.”* Link it to the hook: the alarm rang before anyone touched the pinecone. Name **dread**, the fear of waiting, and **negativity bias**, imagining disasters when unsure.

steps.purpose: Name the brain system behind what students felt in the hook.
students: Why might the alarm ring louder for a box than for a spider you can see?

steps.title: Choose a handout
script: Students choose a handout. All three work from the class’s votes and the studies the exhibition reports.

levels.name: Green Level
levels.summary: Record the class’s votes on three choices beside the studies’ results, match four new words to their meanings, read the 2014 study’s counts as fractions, and write a claim with evidence.

levels.name: Yellow Level
levels.summary: Tabulate all six votes as percentages, take apart the 2014 and 2020 studies (what changed, what was measured, how many took part), and explain why the marble jar choice shows ambiguity aversion.

levels.name: Red Level
levels.summary: Design an experiment to test whether not knowing raises a pulse, with a clear box and a covered box, then make it fair and kind, and judge what a poster leaves out when it says “some people.”

steps.purpose: Read fear studies as a scientist, at the right level of challenge.
students: Choose Green, Yellow or Red. All three use the class’s votes and the exhibition’s studies.

steps.title: Would you believe it?
script: Ask: *“A study says people chose the scary option. What would you want to know before you believed it?”* Red-level students share a design and how they made it kind.

screen.question: A study says people chose the scary option. What would you want to know before you believed it?

steps.purpose: Turn the lesson into a habit: ask what a study changed, measured and counted.
students: How many people?
What was changed, and what was measured?
Would it work the same in our class?

steps.title: Look back
script: Then ask the objectives back as questions: *“Can you now…?”* Students show a thumb up, sideways or down. Exit ticket: *“Why can a box you can’t see into feel scarier than a spider you can?”*
